laws.rule: Penalties for drug offences are severe and can lead to life in jail. Cyprus has a strictly enforced zero-tolerance policy towards illegal drugs, including laughing gas and cannabis. Carrying even small amounts of an illegal drug can result in jail time. You should expect severe penalties such as a lengthy jail sentence and heavy fines for possessing, using or smuggling illegal drugs, including when transiting through the airport.
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: Buying property in north Cyprus can be risky and should be avoided, as legal titles to land can be uncertain. Since the 1974 conflict, many displaced people in the north have maintained property ownership claims. It's a crime to buy, sell or rent property without the owner's consent. Get legal advice before signing a property contract. It's also a crime to intend to purchase disputed property. Officials may consider your possession of property pamphlets from the north as evidence of intent to purchase. Equally, land registry documents from the south should not be carried into the north, as this has led to arrests by authorities in the north. You could face criminal proceedings if you cross t
laws.heading: Buying property

laws.rule: It's illegal in both parts of Cyprus to: take photos of military camps, facilities, personnel or equipment, even by accident take photos in the UN Buffer Zone take photos in any military-designated area enter a restricted military zone export cultural or archaeological artefacts without official authorisation
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: If you plan to get married, check the legal requirements with the local municipality where your wedding will take place before you travel. Cypriot authorities will not accept Certificates of No Impediment to Marry (CNI) issued outside Australia.
laws.heading: Marriage laws

laws.rule: The Australian High Commission can't assist with surrogacy arrangements, provide legal advice, or recommend hospitals or clinics. Due to possible legal complications, Australians considering surrogacy should confirm the exact location of the clinic, hospital, or treatment facility on the island before proceeding.
laws.heading: Surrogacy

laws.rule: Surrogacy in the Republic of Cyprus is highly regulated and subject to strict conditions. Be aware that non-compliance with Cypriot laws on surrogacy could lead to criminal penalties. Before proceeding, seek independent legal advice on both Australian and Cypriot laws.
laws.heading: Surrogacy in the Republic of Cyprus

laws.rule: You should avoid pursuing surrogacy arrangements in northern Cyprus. Intending parents should be aware that there is a high level of risk involved and that there are public concerns about human rights abuses, sexual exploitation, criminal networks, and a lack of adequate legal protections for all parties involved. Additionally, the Australian High Commission's ability to assist Australian citizens in northern Cyprus is limited.
laws.heading: Surrogacy in the north (the area not controlled by the Government of the Republic of Cyprus)

laws.rule: Same-sex relationships are legal in the Republic of Cyprus, and Civil Unions are recognised. However, they may not be as widely accepted as in Australia. Same-sex relationships’ are also legal in the north of Cyprus but not widely accepted.
laws.heading: LGBTQIA+ travellers

laws.rule: Dual Australian-Cypriot nationals may have to do national military service. This may apply if you're: male aged 15 to 50 years staying longer than 3 months Female dual nationals may have civil defence obligations. This may apply if you're: female aged 18 to 50 years a permanent resident of Cyprus If you're a male dual national aged 16 to 26 years, you need an exit permit to leave Cyprus. You can get a permit from either the: Check with the Ministry of Defence before you travel.
laws.heading: National military service in the Republic of Cyprus

laws.rule: If you're in north Cyprus, you might have to do military service if you: have a Turkish-Cypriot background are male are older than 18 years stay longer than 3 months in north Cyprus Check with the relevant authorities (Turkish Cypriot) before you travel.
laws.heading: National military service in the north

laws.rule: Officials may reduce the length of your national service if you show evidence of long-term residency in Australia. Get a copy of your movements in and out of Australia as evidence of residency. Make a 'Request for International Movement Records' to the Department of Home Affairs. You'll need this documentation if you: are or could be a dual national haven't completed national service intend to stay longer than 3 months - Advice for dual nationals
laws.heading: Length of national military service

laws.rule: You can only use your Australian driver's licence for 6 months from your date of arrival. You'll need to obtain a local driving licence to continue to drive after 6 months. To get a local licence, refer to the Road Transport Department. The minimum age for driving is 18 years.
laws.heading: Driving permit

laws.rule: The Department of Civil Aviation's guidance for visitors says not to fly in no-fly zones and to keep at least 8 km from airports and heliports; flights in airport geographical zones need an operational authorisation applied for at least 14 days ahead.

Anyone entering or leaving Cyprus carrying cash of EUR 10,000 or more (about A$15,900 at the RBA rate of 30 October 2026, A$1 = EUR 0.6293) must declare it in writing to a customs officer. Cash includes currency, bearer instruments, coins with at least 90% gold and gold bullion of at least 99.5%. Failing to declare, or an incomplete or false declaration, is an offence: the cash can be seized, and the penalty on investigation can be up to three years in prison, a fine up to EUR 100,000, or both.
laws.heading: Cash declaration

laws.rule: Arriving from outside the EU, the EU duty-free allowance is 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer, plus one of: 1 litre of spirits over 22% alcohol, or 2 litres of fortified or sparkling wine. The EU page tells travellers to check the destination country's customs for the latest limits.
laws.heading: Duty-free alcohol from outside the EU

laws.rule: Arriving from outside the EU, the EU allowance is 200 cigarettes, 100 cigarillos, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco. The EU page says a lower limit (40 cigarettes, 20 cigarillos, 10 cigars or 50 g of tobacco) applies to land and sea travellers in some EU countries; check this country's customs. You can mix product types but the total must stay within the limit.
laws.heading: Duty-free tobacco from outside the EU

laws.rule: Travelling into the EU from a non-EU country, you are not allowed to bring any meat or dairy products. Limited amounts of fruit and vegetables, eggs, egg products, honey and some fish are allowed. Exceptions: up to 10 kg per person from the Faroe Islands or Greenland, and up to 2 kg of powdered infant milk, infant food or special medical foods (unopened, shelf-stable, proprietary brand), or health-related pet food for an accompanying pet. Undeclared products are confiscated and destroyed, and a fine or prosecution is possible.
laws.heading: Meat and dairy from outside the EU

drone-pilot-pathway.summary: EU baseline (EASA): register once as an operator in the state of residence or establishment, recognised across EASA states; Specific-category work in another state needs cross-border acceptance by that state's authority. National register, zone map and visitor rules checked 6 Nov 2026 (see items); footage routes not yet checked.

register.name: Department of Civil Aviation drones portal

items.text: Not yet checked: whether the national aviation authority publishes a list of authorised operators.

EU rules (Regulations 2019/947 and 2019/945): operators register in the EASA state where they reside or are established; Specific-category operations need an operational authorisation or a standard-scenario declaration.

An operator registered in another EASA state may fly here; for Specific-category work it first gets the authorisation or STS declaration at home, then the destination authority must confirm the cross-border operation before flying. Rules for operators from outside EASA states: not yet checked.
Not yet checked: national tourism board or film commission media libraries.

Cyprus's Department of Civil Aviation registers operators on drones.gov.cy. Non-EU visitors flying in Cyprus for the first time register there for EUR 15 (A$23.84 at EUR 0.6293 per A$1, RBA 30 Oct 2026), payable by Visa card only. The minimum age is 18. Someone who has already flown in another EU country must not register again.
A non-EU visitor needs a Remote Pilot Certificate issued by an EU country (the A1/A3 online course and exam is the usual route, valid 5 years).

The department's guidance says not to fly in no-fly zones and to stay at least 8 km from airports and heliports. Flights in airport geographical zones need an operational authorisation, applied for at least 14 days ahead with third-party insurance of at least EUR 1,000,000. The map itself was not found on the pages read.
